passage.title: A Town That Repaired Its River

paragraphs.text: In the fictional town of Millhaven, a narrow river runs between the market and the primary school. For many years, people watched small fish from the footbridge and ate lunch on the bank. Then plastic bags and food containers began collecting beside the bridge. The town organized a Saturday cleanup, and sixty people arrived with gloves and large sacks. By the afternoon, the river looked much better. Photographs of the volunteers appeared in the local newsletter. Three weeks later, however, the same corner was covered with waste again. Some residents blamed the people who used the riverside path, but nobody had actually followed the rubbish to its source.

The council first responded by planning a larger cleanup every month. A shop owner, Mara Bell, questioned this decision. Her store stood upstream, away from the popular walking path, and she often saw packaging move past her back door after rain. She suggested that the school and the shops record where rubbish appeared before deciding what to do. The head teacher agreed, provided that the children stayed out of the water. Small groups watched from safe locations with adults. They visited on dry mornings and again after showers. They counted large pieces of waste, noted their type, and marked the observations on a map.

The observations challenged the original explanation. On dry days, the river near the walking path contained little new rubbish. After heavy rain, much more packaging arrived from two narrow channels above the market. These channels carried rainwater from streets into the river. They did not begin at the footbridge. The children also noticed that the waste included thin wrapping paper used by market sellers. This did not prove that sellers were throwing paper directly into the river. It did show that the council needed to examine how packaging was stored and collected. Watching the busiest place alone had hidden what was happening farther upstream.

A second visit revealed a practical problem behind the shops. Sellers placed their waste in open baskets while waiting for the evening collection. Some baskets stood under the edge of a roof, but others were completely exposed. Wind moved light packaging across the yard, and rain then carried it into the street channels. The collection workers were usually on time. Moving their visit earlier would therefore not solve the problem on its own, because rubbish was left outside throughout the day. Mara proposed covered containers for the shared yard. She also asked sellers to keep clean packaging indoors until they were ready to put it inside a container.

The council had limited money, so it tried the proposal behind four shops before buying equipment for the whole market. Each shop received a covered container, but the first week brought a surprise. One container remained almost empty while loose paper lay beside it. Its lid was difficult to open while carrying a large box. A worker sometimes left the lid raised rather than opening it repeatedly. The container's position also blocked part of a delivery route. Instead of blaming the worker, the trial team changed the handle and moved the container beside the sorting table. After those changes, the shops used it regularly.

The school continued its observations for another month. The children used the same places and counting method as before, so the new records could be compared with the earlier ones. There were fewer large pieces of packaging below the market after rain, although the river was not completely clean. Fallen branches still caught bottles that had entered from other streets. The volunteers removed those bottles during a smaller cleanup. Nobody claimed that covered containers had solved every kind of river pollution. The trial concerned visible rubbish from one market yard, not water quality or waste from every part of the town. This limit mattered when the council explained its results.

Some residents worried that the school project would replace the volunteer cleanups. Mara explained that the two activities had different purposes. Cleanups removed waste already in the river and helped people notice the problem. Better storage reduced the amount of new waste entering from the market. The council kept a cleanup at the start of each school term, but it stopped planning larger monthly events as its main response. It used the money saved to improve containers in other shared yards. Sellers were asked to report broken lids quickly. Collection workers added the condition of the containers to their normal inspection, without taking responsibility for every loose piece of paper.

By the following spring, the footbridge again offered a clear view of the water most days. The town still held river events, but the newsletter no longer treated the number of sacks collected as its only measure of success. It also reported whether new rubbish appeared after rain. The project had begun with an attractive public activity and ended with changes that were less easy to photograph: suitable handles, dry storage, and regular checks. Cooperation remained important, but cooperation worked better when people understood how the waste moved. Millhaven had not simply found more volunteers. It had learned to connect a visible problem with an ordinary practice that was causing it.

questions.stem: Why did the team focus on waste storage behind the shops?

choices.text: Rubbish returned after the cleanup because waste collection visits left the shared yard uninspected for weeks.
choices.text_ja: 清掃後にごみが戻ってきたのは、回収業者の訪問後も共用の庭が何週間も点検されないままだったからだ。

choices.text: Packaging caught in branches suggested that bottles from other streets were the main source of market waste.
choices.text_ja: 枝に引っかかった包装材から、市場のごみの主な発生源は他の通りから流れてくるボトルだと考えられたからだ。

choices.text: Rain carried exposed market packaging through upstream street channels, linking the observations to storage behind the shops.
choices.text_ja: 雨で、むき出しの市場の包装材が上流の街路の水路を通って運ばれており、その観察結果が店の裏手での保管状況と結びついたからだ。

choices.text: Market wrapping in the channels suggested that sellers were putting used paper directly into the water.
choices.text_ja: 水路で見つかった市場の包装紙から、売り手が使用済みの紙を直接水に捨てていると考えられたからだ。

questions.stem_ja: チームが店の裏手のごみの保管状況に注目したのはなぜか。

questions.stem: What change made one trial container easier to use?

choices.text: The team changed its handle and left it beside the sheltered edge of the roof.
choices.text_ja: チームは取っ手を変え、屋根の庇の下の屋根のある場所の脇に置いたままにした。

choices.text: The team moved it beside the sorting table and made room by widening the delivery route.
choices.text_ja: チームは容器を仕分け台の脇に移し、搬入経路を広げて場所を確保した。

choices.text: The team moved it indoors and changed its handle so workers could carry boxes more easily.
choices.text_ja: チームは容器を屋内に移し、作業員が箱をより楽に運べるよう取っ手を変えた。

choices.text: The team changed the handle and moved the container beside the sorting table, encouraging regular use.
choices.text_ja: チームは取っ手を変えたうえで容器を仕分け台の脇に移し、日常的に使われやすくした。

questions.stem_ja: 試験用の容器の1つを使いやすくしたのはどんな変更か。

questions.stem: How did cleanups and better storage serve different purposes?

choices.text: Cleanups identified the market's waste source, while better storage supplied the records used to compare rainwater quality.
choices.text_ja: 清掃は市場のごみの発生源を特定し、保管の改善は雨水の水質を比べるための記録をもたらした。

choices.text: Cleanups removed existing river waste, while covered storage reduced the market packaging entering after wind and rain.
choices.text_ja: 清掃は川にすでにあるごみを取り除き、屋根付きの保管は風雨のあとに流れ込む市場の包装材を減らした。

choices.text: Cleanups removed the market's recent waste, while storage reduced bottles entering the river from the other streets.
choices.text_ja: 清掃は市場の最近のごみを取り除き、保管の改善は他の通りから川に入るボトルを減らした。

choices.text: Cleanups kept the market's containers usable, while storage made the volunteers' later river inspections less frequent.
choices.text_ja: 清掃は市場の容器を使える状態に保ち、保管の改善はボランティアによる後の川の点検の回数を減らした。

questions.stem_ja: 清掃活動と保管の改善は、それぞれどのような異なる目的を果たしたか。

questions.stem: Why does the author explain what the trial did not measure?

choices.text: To distinguish findings about visible market rubbish from improvements in other kinds of river pollution.
choices.text_ja: 目に見える市場のごみに関する知見と、他の種類の川の汚染に関する改善とを区別するため。

choices.text: To identify the other streets as the next source to which the market's results applied.
choices.text_ja: 他の通りを、市場での結果が当てはまる次の発生源として特定するため。

choices.text: To justify extending the successful container trial to the water-quality problems elsewhere in town.
choices.text_ja: 成功した容器の試験を、町の他の場所の水質問題にも広げることを正当化するため。

choices.text: To explain why the remaining bottles made comparisons with the earlier observations less useful.
choices.text_ja: 残っているボトルのせいで、以前の観察との比較が役に立たなくなった理由を説明するため。

questions.stem_ja: 筆者が、試験では測定しなかったことを説明しているのはなぜか。

questions.stem: What best describes the lesson of Millhaven’s project?

choices.text: Public cleanups remained the central response, with suitable containers helping volunteers remove larger quantities of river waste.
choices.text_ja: 公共の清掃活動が対応の中心であり続け、適切な容器がボランティアによる川のごみのより多くの除去を助けた。

choices.text: Preventing new waste became possible when collections were brought forward and containers were moved closer to shops.
choices.text_ja: 回収を前倒しし、容器を店の近くに移したことで、新たなごみの発生を防ぐことが可能になった。

choices.text: Regular collection became more effective after workers took over the school observations and traced the channels upstream.
choices.text_ja: 作業員が学校の観察を引き継ぎ、上流の水路をたどったあと、定期的な回収がより効果的になった。

choices.text: The town combined removing existing rubbish with changes to market storage that reduced waste entering after rain.
choices.text_ja: 町は、すでにあるごみの除去と、雨のあとに流れ込むごみを減らす市場の保管方法の変更とを組み合わせた。

paragraphs.text: The children of the fictional Vale District could borrow books from a modern library in the central town. For families living near the town square, this was convenient. For those on distant farms, a visit required a long journey and usually an adult who could drive. Teachers noticed that children often returned to school after holidays without having opened a new book. A district officer proposed a mobile library: a small bus fitted with shelves. It would visit three villages every fortnight. The district expected that bringing more books closer to the children would quickly increase reading. At first, the plan was judged mainly by the number of books borrowed.

The bus carried adventure stories, simple science books, picture books, and short accounts of local history. Its first visits were busy. Teachers brought classes to the village stops, and children chose books with bright covers. Over the first two months, borrowing rose sharply. The officer considered adding another stop and using the same bus to serve more families. However, some teachers had noticed a different pattern. Several children returned books without remembering much about them. Others borrowed the same kind of book each time but said they lost interest after a few pages. A high borrowing total showed that the books reached children. It did not show how often they were read.

One teacher, Iona Reed, asked families what happened after the bus left. Some children enjoyed reading alone. Others wanted to talk about difficult words or surprising parts of a story, but their parents were busy when they arrived home. A few children chose books that looked exciting but were harder than they expected. Parents did not ask for a larger collection as their first priority. They asked for help choosing books and a chance for children to share what they had read. Iona suggested a short reading circle at each stop. Children could listen to a few pages, talk about them, and then choose a book to take home.

The district did not have enough money to hire a teacher to travel with the bus. Instead, Iona trained a village volunteer at each existing stop. The volunteers learned to ask questions that had more than one possible personal response, such as which part had surprised a reader. They were told not to turn the circle into another school test. The driver helped display books but remained responsible for the vehicle and borrowing records. The first circles lasted twenty minutes, during the bus's usual visit. This meant that the project improved support at the existing stops before trying to reach an additional village.

The circles soon revealed a weakness in the timetable. The bus arrived at Brook End just before many children returned from school. A few families could collect books, but most missed the discussion. Borrowing there had been lower than at the other stops, and the officer had originally thought local families were less interested in reading. Iona's interviews showed that several children regularly walked past the empty meeting room after the bus had gone. The driver could not simply stay longer because another village expected the bus later. The district therefore changed the order of the route, visiting Brook End last rather than first.

Attendance at Brook End improved after the change. Nevertheless, the volunteers resisted judging success only by how many children came to each circle. Some children attended every meeting but read very little between visits. Others came less often and finished books at home. Volunteers kept short notes on whether children could describe a passage, explain a choice of book, or ask about something they did not understand. These were observations, not marks or a competition. Children could bring an unfinished book and discuss why they had stopped. In several cases, hearing another child's description encouraged a reluctant reader to try a different book rather than give up reading altogether.

After six months, borrowing was still higher than before the bus arrived, but the number of books borrowed per visit had stopped rising. The officer initially saw this as a warning. Iona offered a different explanation. Children were now more careful about their choices, and some kept longer books across two visits. Interviews and volunteer notes suggested that more borrowed books were actually being read. The district did not claim that the reading circles had improved every child's school results. It had not collected suitable evidence for that claim. It did conclude that borrowing figures needed to be considered alongside information about how the books were used.

The district kept the bus and the three stops. It postponed the proposed fourth stop until it could find another vehicle or a timetable that would not shorten the circles. Families in the unserved village were understandably disappointed, so the officer explained the choice publicly rather than calling the project complete. Access to books remained a real need. Yet the bus had shown that access was more than placing shelves close to a child's home. A useful service also had to arrive at the right time and offer support that children could continue using. The library on wheels worked best when its route and its conversations were planned together.

questions.stem: What did the district learn about improving children’s reading?

choices.text: Bringing books closer helped, but attendance figures provided the clearest measure of reading improvement.
choices.text_ja: 本を近くに届けることは役立ったが、読書の改善を測る最も明確な指標は参加者数だった。

choices.text: Nearby books improved access, but choosing support, discussions, and suitable arrival times also influenced reading.

choices.text_ja: 本を近くに届けることは役立ったが、貸出数を伸ばし続けるにはより難しい本を増やす必要があった。

choices.text: Bringing books closer helped, but serving another village was the next step toward deeper reading.
choices.text_ja: 本を近くに届けることは役立ったが、より深い読書への次の一歩は別の村にもサービスを広げることだった。

questions.stem_ja: 子どもの読書を向上させることについて、地区は何を学んだか。

questions.stem: Why did the bus begin visiting Brook End last?

choices.text: Its earlier arrival made it difficult for the driver to finish loans before the discussion began.
choices.text_ja: 到着が早いと、話し合いが始まる前に運転手が貸出を終えるのが難しかったから。

choices.text_ja: 到着が早いと、子どもたちが停車場所に来る前にボランティアが研修を受ける時間が足りなかったから。

choices.text: Its earlier arrival kept the bus from leaving enough books for children who stayed at home.
choices.text_ja: 到着が早いと、家にいる子どものための本をバスが十分に置いていけなかったから。

choices.text: The bus left before many children returned from school, preventing their participation in Brook End's discussion.
choices.text_ja: バスは多くの子どもが学校から戻る前に去ってしまい、ブルック・エンドの話し合いに参加できなかったから。

questions.stem_ja: なぜバスはブルック・エンドを最後に訪れるようになったのか。

questions.stem: How did the district provide staff for the reading circles?

choices.text: Iona trained village discussion leaders, while the driver remained responsible for the bus and its records.
choices.text_ja: アイオナが村の話し合いの進行役を研修し、運転手は引き続きバスとその記録に責任を持った。

choices.text: Each village recruited a volunteer whom the driver trained during the bus's regular visits.
choices.text_ja: 各村がボランティアを募り、その人たちをバスの通常の訪問中に運転手が研修した。

choices.text: The driver led the circles after local volunteers took over the vehicle and borrowing records.
choices.text_ja: 地元のボランティアが車両と貸出記録を引き継いだ後、運転手が読書会を進行した。

choices.text: A teacher travelled between villages to lead the circles while volunteers handled the borrowing records.
choices.text_ja: 教師が村々を移動して読書会を進行し、ボランティアが貸出記録を扱った。

questions.stem_ja: 地区は読書会の運営人員をどのように確保したか。

questions.stem: Why was slower growth in borrowing not enough to judge the project?

choices.text: Steady borrowing suggested that children had reached a similar level of interest at the three stops.
choices.text_ja: 貸出数が横ばいであることは、三つの停車場所で子どもたちの関心が同程度に達したことを示していた。

choices.text: Longer loans suggested that the circles were completing more of the reading during each bus visit.
choices.text_ja: 貸出期間が長くなったことは、バスの訪問ごとに読書会が読書をより多く終わらせていることを示していた。

choices.text: Careful choices and longer loans could slow borrowing growth while more books were actually being read.
choices.text_ja: 本を慎重に選び、貸出期間を長くすると、貸出数の伸びが鈍っても、実際に読まれる本は増えることがある。

choices.text: Volunteer notes suggested that improved book choices were already producing better results in school tests.
choices.text_ja: ボランティアの記録は、本選びの改善がすでに学校のテストでより良い結果を生んでいることを示していた。

questions.stem_ja: なぜ貸出数の伸びの鈍化だけでは、この事業を判断するのに十分でなかったのか。

questions.stem: Why mention that a child could discuss an unfinished book?

choices.text: To show how discussing a difficulty helped volunteers decide whether to extend the child's loan.
choices.text_ja: 困りごとを話し合うことで、ボランティアが子どもの貸出期間を延長するか判断しやすくなったことを示すため。

choices.text: To show how volunteers used personal responses to judge which children had improved their reading.
choices.text_ja: ボランティアが個人的な感想をもとに、どの子の読書が向上したかを判断したことを示すため。

choices.text: To illustrate support for difficulties and renewed reading interest without making book completion a participation test.
choices.text_ja: 読み終えることを参加の条件にせずに、つまずきへの支援と読書への関心の再燃を支えたことを示すため。

choices.text: To show how children could help volunteers replace difficult books with simpler titles at each stop.
choices.text_ja: 各停車場所で、子どもたちが本をやさしい本に入れ替えるのをボランティアに手伝えたことを示すため。

questions.stem_ja: なぜ、子どもが読み終えていない本について話してもよいと述べているのか。

paragraphs.text: A plant cannot walk away when the place around it becomes crowded. Its seeds, however, may travel. Moving seeds away from a parent plant is called seed dispersal. Wind, water, and animals can carry seeds into places that the parent itself could never reach. It is tempting to imagine a simple competition in which the seed traveling farthest is the winner. That picture leaves out an important second part of the journey. A seed must arrive where it can begin growing, and the young plant must then survive. Comparing methods of travel therefore means asking not only how seeds move, but also where each method is likely to leave them.

Some seeds have structures that help them move through air. A dandelion seed, for example, is attached to a small group of fine hairs. Other wind-carried seeds have wing-like shapes. These structures help movement, but wind does not choose a comfortable home for the seed. Imagine two seeds from the same plant landing after the same breeze. One comes to rest in a patch of open soil, while the other falls on a paved path. This is a hypothetical comparison, not the result of a particular experiment. The second seed might have traveled farther, yet its greater distance alone would not make its destination better for growth.

Water offers a different route. Some fruits or seeds float, and a current may carry them away. Coconuts are a familiar example of a fruit that can be carried by water. The direction of a river or movement along a shore can influence the places reached. This makes water travel different from movement through the air above a field. A floating object does not have access to every nearby dry patch simply because that patch would support a plant. It follows the water until it is left somewhere. For a successful new plant, the place where the journey ends still matters, along with whether the seed remains able to grow.

Animals move seeds in more than one way. Some eat fruit and later leave seeds elsewhere in their droppings. The edible part of the fruit attracts the animal, while some seeds can survive passing through its body. Other seeds attach to fur or clothing and are carried until they come loose. Animals may also collect seeds as food and bury them. Some stored seeds are not recovered and may later grow. These routes are different: a seed inside a fruit is not using the same mechanism as one caught on fur. The animal's habits influence the journey in each case, including where it feeds, travels, rests, or stores food.

To compare these routes fairly, consider an imagined landscape with a pond, a paved road, and a strip of woodland. The example is a teaching model, not a claim about a real research site. Wind might carry a light seed over the road, but the seed could land on a surface with little suitable soil. Water might move a floating fruit around the pond while never carrying it into the woodland. An animal that feeds beside the pond and rests under trees might connect those two places. None of these movements guarantees growth. Each opens certain possible routes and leaves other routes unlikely or unavailable.

Arrival is not the same as germination, the stage when a seed begins to develop into a plant. Conditions such as water and temperature matter, and requirements differ among plants. Some seeds do not start growing immediately even when they reach soil. Their outer coats or other features can delay the process until suitable conditions are met. After a seedling emerges, it also needs resources and space. A place that is easy to reach can still be too crowded or unsuitable. Conversely, remaining near the parent is not automatically a failure, although competition there may make growth difficult. The full story extends beyond the moment when a seed lands.

A useful observation would therefore distinguish several events: departure from the parent, arrival at a destination, germination, and survival of the seedling. Suppose an observer counted many seeds on the far side of the imagined road. That would support a statement about arrival, not yet a statement about how many new plants grew there. If the observer later found only a few seedlings, more questions would follow. Were the seeds unable to germinate, or did seedlings emerge and then die? Without further observations, those possibilities should not be treated as the same explanation. Counting one stage carefully is valuable, but it does not replace evidence about the next stage.

There is consequently no single travel method that should be called best for every environment. Wind-carried seeds, floating fruits, and animal-carried seeds meet different opportunities and limits. Their advantages depend partly on the landscape and on the plants' growth requirements. Distance remains useful information: it can describe movement away from crowded ground or entry into a new area. Yet distance should be understood as one part of a longer process, rather than as a final score. Seeds that travel far may reach promising places, unsuitable places, or places whose value changes with the conditions. Understanding dispersal means connecting a way of moving with the possibility of a new plant becoming established.

questions.stem: Which comparison between dispersal methods matches the passage?

choices.text: Water carries seeds through waterways, whereas animals can connect feeding and resting places in different habitats.
choices.text_ja: 水は水路を通って種子を運ぶ一方、動物は異なる生息地にある採食の場と休息の場を結びつけることがある。

choices.text: Water follows shorelines toward dry ground, whereas animals tend to deposit seeds near the plants where they feed.
choices.text_ja: 水は岸沿いに乾いた地面へ向かって進む一方、動物は餌を食べる植物の近くに種子を落とす傾向がある。

choices.text: Wind and water depend on seed shape, whereas animal routes depend chiefly on whether seeds survive digestion.
choices.text_ja: 風と水は種子の形に左右される一方、動物による経路は主に種子が消化を生き延びるかどうかに左右される。

choices.text: Wind crosses barriers between habitats, whereas water and animals mainly spread seeds within the habitat of the parent.
choices.text_ja: 風は生息地間の障壁を越える一方、水と動物は主に親植物の生息地の中で種子を広げる。

questions.stem_ja: 次の散布方法の比較のうち、本文に合うものはどれか。

questions.stem: How can an animal’s stored food contribute to seed dispersal?

choices.text: Some seeds buried as food may remain unrecovered and later grow in the animal's storage place.
choices.text_ja: 食料として埋められた種子の一部は回収されないままになり、後に動物の貯蔵場所で育つことがある。

choices.text: Some buried seeds may become easier to digest after they remain in the storage place.
choices.text_ja: 埋められた種子の一部は、貯蔵場所に置かれたままでいるうちに消化しやすくなることがある。

choices.text: Some buried seeds may begin growing after the animal retrieves them from its storage place.
choices.text_ja: 埋められた種子の一部は、動物が貯蔵場所から取り出した後に成長し始めることがある。

choices.text: Some buried seeds may travel farther when the animal returns to dig up the young plants.
choices.text_ja: 埋められた種子の一部は、動物が若い植物を掘り起こしに戻ると、さらに遠くへ運ばれることがある。

questions.stem_ja: 動物が蓄えた食料は、どのように種子散布に役立ちうるか。

questions.stem: What can a large count of seeds across the road establish on its own?

choices.text: Many seeds reached usable soil there, but the count does not establish how long seedlings survived.
choices.text_ja: 多くの種子が使える土に届いたが、その数は苗がどれだけ長く生き残ったかを確かめるものではない。

choices.text: Many seeds began growing there, but the count does not establish why some seedlings later died.
choices.text_ja: 多くの種子がそこで成長し始めたが、その数は一部の苗が後に枯れた理由を確かめるものではない。

passage.title: How Public Clocks Changed Town Life

paragraphs.text: A clock displayed above a square can seem like an ordinary piece of street furniture. Before personal timepieces became widely available, however, a public clock gave many people access to information they could not easily obtain for themselves. Bells could announce a time without requiring listeners to see a dial, and daylight could help people organize familiar activities. A visible clock added another way to coordinate the day. Its value did not lie simply in having a moving hand. People could refer to the same display when arranging meetings, opening shops, or deciding when a particular task should begin. A public clock could turn private guesses into a shared reference.

Having a shared reference within a town did not necessarily mean sharing time with another town. Local time could be based on the Sun's position, and local noon differed between places at different longitudes. For activities contained within one community, this difference might cause little difficulty. Wider travel made it more noticeable. A passenger reading a railway timetable needed to know which time the printed figures represented. In nineteenth-century Britain, railway companies increasingly used Greenwich Mean Time as a common standard. The Royal Observatory's account notes that most railway companies had adopted it by the 1840s. A connected transport system gave people a practical reason to compare clocks across locations.

Consider a hypothetical market town whose public clock shows one time while its station uses another. This is an explanatory example, not the history of a named town. A shopkeeper tells a customer to collect a parcel at noon and then catch a train. The customer might correctly understand the shopkeeper's noon yet misread how it fits the railway departure. Neither clock has to be broken for the plan to fail. The problem is that the two arrangements use different references. Making the customer walk faster would not remove the confusion. The references themselves need to be understood or brought into agreement.

A common standard can make such arrangements easier, but it does not tell everyone when to work. Imagine the same town adopting station time for its public clock. People can now compare the shop's opening and the train's departure without translating between two clocks. The baker may still begin work before the shop assistant, and a farmer may still adjust outdoor work to daylight or weather. Agreeing about what an hour is called does not require every activity to occur at that hour. This distinction is useful because standard time can be confused with a single schedule imposed on all residents.

Public clocks also connect time with places. A dial above a square can be read by someone nearby, but not necessarily by a person in a distant workshop or a home behind the buildings. A bell spreads information differently: listeners can hear it without looking toward the square, although a striking bell cannot continuously display the minutes between its signals. These are practical differences between ways of sharing time. They help explain why a town might use more than one device. Installing a prominent clock does not automatically give every resident equally convenient access to it. The location and form of the signal matter alongside the accuracy of the mechanism.

Imagine a worker who normally starts an outdoor task once the ground is light enough to see safely. A shop might announce its opening by the public clock, while the worker's first task still follows daylight. In this example, the clock helps coordinate a later delivery without determining the best time for the earlier outdoor work. The example does not show that one worker is careless about time or that one method is always superior. Different activities need different kinds of information. Trouble arises when someone assumes that the same schedule must suit them all simply because they can read the same clock.

When discussing these changes, it is helpful to separate three questions. First, is a timepiece working accurately enough for its purpose? Second, do the relevant timepieces follow the same reference? Third, can the people involved obtain and use the information at suitable moments? A repaired mechanism addresses the first question. Agreement between a station clock and a town clock addresses the second. A visible dial, a useful signal, or clear timetable information can help address the third. Improving one does not guarantee that the other two are settled. A technically good clock may therefore fail to prevent missed arrangements if communication remains confusing.

The wider significance of public clocks is that they made coordination more visible and, in suitable circumstances, more convenient. Shops and transport could connect activities through a common reference rather than through separate estimates of the hour. Yet the benefits depended on how that reference reached people and on what they were trying to do. A clock did not remove weather, distance, or differences between kinds of work. It offered a tool around which new arrangements could be made. Understanding its social role means examining those arrangements as well as the mechanism inside the case. Shared time helped people cooperate, but shared time was never the same thing as an identical day for everyone.

passage.title: A New Route to the Clinic

paragraphs.text: The fictional village of Alder Vale stands beyond a line of low hills. Its nearest clinic is in the market town of Fenwick. People with cars can reach the clinic without much trouble, but other residents often depend on relatives or neighbors. The village council learned that several people had missed routine appointments because they could not arrange a lift. It decided to test a small bus service twice a week. Council members wanted to keep the fare low, believing that transport costs were the main reason residents delayed visits. The bus would stop near the village shop, carry passengers to the clinic, and bring them home on the same day.

The first timetable seemed simple. The bus left Alder Vale at nine in the morning and returned from Fenwick at noon. The clinic normally opened before the bus arrived, so council members thought passengers would have enough time. Posters appeared in the shop, and a volunteer explained how to reserve a seat by telephone. The fare was less than residents usually paid to share a taxi. During the first month, however, most seats remained empty. A council member suggested reducing the fare again. Another proposed ending the service before it used more money. Neither had yet spoken to the residents who had originally asked for help.

The council asked a community worker, Lea Morgan, to make those conversations part of the review. She contacted people who had missed appointments and also spoke to the clinic receptionist. Residents generally knew about the bus and considered its price reasonable. Their main concern was the return journey. Many available appointments were in the late morning or early afternoon. A passenger whose consultation finished after noon had no bus home. Even an earlier appointment might run late. People were not willing to use the bus if they might have to pay for a taxi on the return trip. A cheap outward journey was not enough to make the whole visit affordable.

One resident's experience made the problem clear. Mr. Dene had been offered an appointment at eleven fifteen. The outward bus would get him there in good time, but he could not be certain that his consultation would finish before noon. He asked for an earlier appointment and learned that those times were often taken by patients from other villages. He therefore arranged a lift with his niece instead of using the service. This did not mean he preferred traveling by car. He needed a reliable way back. Lea reported his experience as an example of the timetable problem, without sharing his private medical information.

The council considered several changes. A second bus could offer more journeys, but the trial budget could not cover another vehicle and driver. Asking the first driver to wait all day would also increase the cost. Lea proposed a later return journey and a small group of appointment times reserved for bus passengers on the two service days. The clinic agreed to test the arrangement for routine visits, while keeping urgent care under its usual system. Passengers still had to contact the clinic separately to make appointments. Booking a bus seat would not automatically book a consultation. This distinction appeared clearly on the revised posters.

Under the new timetable, the bus left the village at nine thirty and returned from Fenwick at two thirty. The clinic offered the reserved appointments between ten thirty and one. Passengers had a place to wait near the clinic and could visit nearby shops if they wished. The fare did not change. In the next month, more residents used the bus, including several who had previously borrowed lifts. The council also heard a complaint: people with very early appointments still found the new departure too late. Lea did not present the revised timetable as suitable for every patient. The trial was designed to improve one useful option, not replace every other way of reaching the clinic.

To evaluate the service, the council compared reservations with actual journeys and asked whether users had returned home as planned. It also checked how many reserved appointment times the clinic could continue providing. The number of passengers mattered, but a full bus would not count as success if people regularly missed consultations or became stranded afterward. The council avoided comparing the health of passengers with that of nonusers, because their needs were different and the trial had not been designed to measure health outcomes. Its immediate question was narrower: had the transport arrangement become dependable enough for the appointments it was intended to serve?

After three months, the council kept the revised service for another season. It did not reduce the fare a second time. Instead, it used a small part of the budget to improve telephone booking information and to explain the appointment arrangement to new residents. The experience changed how council members discussed access. Distance and price were important, but they did not describe every barrier. A journey had to fit the activity at its destination and include a realistic return. Alder Vale's bus became useful when the council stopped treating travel and appointments as separate problems. Listening to the people who did not use the service had helped explain what passenger numbers alone could not.

paragraphs.text: At the center of the fictional city of Linton lies Willow Pond, a shallow stretch of water beside a playground. Families enjoy watching birds there, and local children have often found insects among the plants near the edge. After several years of heavy use, parts of the walking path began to break apart. The city decided to repair the path and build a smooth stone wall around most of the pond. Officials expected the work to make the area safer and easier to clean. When the wall was finished, the pond looked tidy. Yet the school nature club soon reported that several familiar kinds of insects were becoming difficult to find.

The club had kept notes during visits before the building work. Its members knew the pond was not exactly the same in every season, so they did not compare a summer visit with a winter one. Their teacher asked them to return during the same weeks in the following year and to observe from the same locations. Birds still landed on the open water, but fewer stayed along the edge. The club found fewer places where small animals could move between land and water. The wall had not made the whole pond lifeless. It had changed one part of the habitat, the area where the water met the bank.

A city gardener explained what had been removed. Before the work, shallow muddy shelves and plants formed an uneven border. Some insects used those plants, and the protected spaces between them offered places to rest or feed. The new wall replaced many of these shelves with a steep edge. Keeping the border clear made cleaning simpler, but it also left less shelter. This explanation did not prove that every missing insect had disappeared because of the wall. Weather and changes elsewhere could also affect animals. It did, however, suggest a specific feature the city could test without removing the repaired path.

The parks office chose a quiet corner for a small restoration. Workers removed a short section of stone below the path and created a gentle, planted slope leading into shallow water. A low fence kept visitors away from the new bank until the plants were established. The path remained behind the fence, allowing families to walk around the pond without stepping into the muddy area. Officials rejected a suggestion to restore the entire edge immediately. They wanted to see whether the small section could support animals while remaining practical to maintain. They also needed to find out whether litter would collect among the new plants.

At first, some visitors disliked the corner. The plants were short and uneven, and fallen leaves were no longer cleared away every morning. A photograph taken from across the water made the bank look less finished than the stone wall. The nature club, however, was interested in different details. It looked for insects on the plants, birds feeding close to the shallow water, and signs of small animals using the sheltered spaces. After several months, the members recorded more insect types in the planted corner than beside a similar length of stone wall. This comparison was more useful than simply counting every animal anywhere in the pond.

The new bank also created a maintenance problem. Wind pushed food wrappers into the plants, where they were harder to reach with the equipment used along the stone wall. One worker proposed cutting the plants down to make collection easier. Instead, the office moved a rubbish bin closer to the nearby picnic area and gave workers a narrow tool for reaching between stems. The club explained to visitors why the leaves and living plants were being left in place while food packaging was removed. The aim was not to leave the corner untouched. It was to distinguish useful shelter from rubbish that could damage or cover it.

The parks office reviewed the trial after a full year. It considered the club's records, workers' reports, and complaints from path users. The planted corner had offered more varied edge habitat, and the revised cleaning method was manageable. The office decided to add two more planted sections, but it kept a stretch of clear stone edge beside the busiest viewing point. Families with pushchairs could still use the repaired path, and visitors had places to see the open water easily. The city did not choose between a completely wild pond and a completely paved one. It used different edges for different needs.

Willow Pond's history became part of the school's lesson on observing change. A neat photograph, the teacher explained, could show how a place looked without showing how it worked for animals. A nature survey also had limits: a single busy afternoon could not describe every season or prove every cause. The club's repeated observations helped the city ask better questions and test a modest change. Safety, cleaning, and habitat were all important, but they did not always improve together. By examining the border of the pond closely, Linton found a way to keep a repaired public space while returning some of the shelter its animals had lost.

paragraphs.text: A phone can stop being useful to its owner before it stops being useful altogether. Someone may want a better camera, a larger screen, or a device that works with new software. The old phone may still switch on and perform basic tasks. Another phone may have a damaged screen but working parts inside it. A third may be beyond safe repair. Putting these different devices into one group called old phones hides differences that matter. Repair, reuse, and recycling are related ways of managing them, but they are not the same activity. The best next step depends on the device's condition and on whether someone can use it safely.

Repair aims to keep a device working as a device. Replacing a broken part may allow an owner to keep using a phone rather than buy another immediately. Before making that decision, the fault needs to be understood. A weak battery is different from a cracked screen, and a software limitation may not be solved by replacing either part. This is not a recommendation to open a damaged device at home. Some batteries are not designed for users to remove, and safety guidance matters. The relevant comparison is between a suitable repair and the practical life it can add, not between the age of two phones alone.

Reuse means that the device continues serving a purpose, perhaps for a different owner. Consider a hypothetical phone that no longer meets a photographer's needs but can still make calls and run the applications another user requires. Passing it on may extend its useful life. That example does not mean every unwanted phone is suitable for donation. A recipient needs an appropriate device, not simply an object that the previous owner wishes to remove from a drawer. Useful information about condition, available functions, and necessary accessories helps make the decision. Keeping an unusable phone in circulation can move the problem to someone else instead of solving it.

Personal information is another consideration before reuse. Devices may contain photographs, messages, saved accounts, or other data. The owner should follow appropriate instructions for protecting or removing that information before transferring the phone. A donation or collection program may have its own procedures, but placing the device in a box does not itself demonstrate that those procedures have occurred. The point is separate from the phone's physical condition. A phone can be suitable for another user's tasks while still containing information that should not be passed along with it. Preparing for reuse therefore involves both the object and the information associated with it.

Recycling has a different goal: recovering useful materials when a device or component is no longer kept in ordinary use. Phones contain several kinds of materials, including valuable metals. These materials are mixed within a product rather than stored as neat separate piles. Collection is consequently a beginning, not proof that every useful substance has already been recovered. Devices need to reach suitable facilities, where materials can be identified, separated, and processed. Some collected items may first be assessed for reuse or repair. Counting everything received as already recycled would combine several stages and make the results look more certain than the records justify.

Batteries require particular care. Many phones contain rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. When batteries or battery-containing devices enter unsuitable waste systems, damage during transport or processing can create a fire risk. The United States Environmental Protection Agency advises consumers not to put these items in household rubbish or ordinary recycling bins. It directs them toward appropriate electronics or battery collection services. A label saying recyclable does not mean a device belongs in every container used for recyclable household materials. This distinction is especially important because sorting systems for common packaging are not the same as systems designed to handle batteries and electronic equipment.

Imagine a collection program reporting one hundred phones received. This number is hypothetical and describes no actual program. Suppose some phones are assessed as usable, some need repair, and others enter material recovery. The total received tells us how many objects reached the collection point. To understand what happened afterward, we need separate information about those routes. We should also ask whether suitable phones actually reached users and whether material recovery was completed. A high collection total can be encouraging without answering every later question. Likewise, the presence of a repair route does not show that all the collected devices were repaired or that every repair was worthwhile.

Managing old phones therefore requires several decisions rather than a single promise that recycling will fix everything. Suitable repair can extend an existing device's life. Useful and safe reuse can provide service to another owner. Proper recycling can recover materials from products that cannot remain in use. These routes depend on practical checks, information handling, and collection systems able to manage the equipment. They can support one another: a program may examine a device before choosing its next route. The important distinction is between choosing an appropriate next use and simply moving an unwanted object away. Following the device beyond the collection box gives a clearer picture of what responsible management has achieved.

paragraphs.text: The fictional Brookfield Farm grows vegetables for shops in a nearby town. During a dry summer, its manager, Nina Cole, learned that the farm would receive less irrigation water than usual. Irrigation means supplying crops with water when rain is not enough. Nina considered buying a new watering system, but the farm could not afford it before the hottest weeks arrived. Her workers suggested moving all watering to the evening, when less water might be lost in the heat. Nina agreed to test the change rather than replace equipment immediately. She also asked the team to keep notes, because saving water would be of little use if the vegetables could no longer grow properly.

The farm had three main growing areas: beans near the packing shed, leafy vegetables beside the road, and young tomato plants on a slightly higher field. Workers had usually run the same kind of watering line for the same length of time in every area. This made the daily schedule easy to remember. During the first week of evening watering, the team reduced the total water used, but the crop areas did not respond in the same way. Soil beside some leafy vegetables remained wet the next afternoon. Meanwhile, several young tomato plants began to wilt before evening. A single convenient schedule was not matching all three areas.

Nina asked workers to check the soil before switching on the water. They learned a simple method for recording whether the soil near the roots felt dry, slightly damp, or wet. They also noted plant size and recent rainfall. These observations were not presented as a scientific measurement of every plant's needs. They were a practical way to avoid treating all fields as identical. The workers made checks at the same depth and similar times so their notes could be compared. They found that the road-side soil stayed damp longer, while the higher tomato field dried faster. Newly planted tomatoes also had different needs from the larger bean plants.

The team then changed the length and frequency of watering by area. The leafy vegetables received a shorter evening session on days when the soil was already damp. The young tomatoes were checked earlier in the day, and their watering was adjusted when the soil dried too much before the evening round. The bean area kept a more regular evening schedule. Nina refused a suggestion to make every session shorter by the same amount. That would be easy to arrange, but it would ignore the differences the workers had just observed. The aim was to remove unnecessary watering, not to reach an equal reduction in every field.

One difficulty appeared during harvest preparation. The worker responsible for the tomatoes sometimes helped in the packing shed and missed a soil check. Another worker then followed the old schedule because it was the only one he remembered. Nina made a waterproof chart showing the checks and recent decisions for each area. Workers added their observations before changing a session, rather than keeping the information in separate notebooks. The chart did not tell them to use exactly the same amount every day. It made the reason for each change visible to whoever was on duty. Sharing information became part of saving water.

At the end of the month, the farm had used less irrigation water than during a similar dry period in its own earlier records. The leafy vegetables remained in good condition, and the young tomatoes recovered after their schedule was adjusted. Nina was pleased but cautious about the comparison. The weather and the number of plants were not identical in the two periods. She therefore avoided announcing an exact percentage that the method would save on any farm. What the records clearly showed was that some sessions had been unnecessary when the soil was still damp. The trial had also revealed a field where cutting water without checking could damage plants.

The water supplier invited Nina to describe the trial at a local meeting. Several listeners expected a presentation about a new machine. Instead, she showed the chart and explained how the team had separated three different growing areas. Evening watering was part of the change, but Nina warned against treating it as a complete solution. A useful watering time still had to be matched to the soil, the plants, and the day's conditions. Another farmer asked whether measuring soil moisture more precisely might help. Nina agreed that better tools could improve decisions, but said the team first needed a clear way to act on the information those tools would provide.

Brookfield later set aside money for improvements to its irrigation equipment. The trial had not persuaded Nina that equipment was unimportant. It had helped her decide what an improvement needed to do: allow separate settings and make checks easier rather than simply send water across every field faster. During the following season, the team kept the chart and revised it as crops changed. Saving water had started with moving a daily task to another time. It became more successful when workers asked where water was needed and shared what they found. The farm's lesson was that a limited budget did not prevent useful action, but useful action required more than one rule for every crop.

paragraphs.text: In this fictional case, the Marston Museum displays objects from everyday life, including cooking tools, clothes, and household furniture. Its director believed the collection was welcoming because visitors did not need to know about famous artists or distant kingdoms. Yet a survey suggested that many people left without understanding why particular objects were important. They remembered shapes and colors but not the stories the museum wanted to explain. The labels beside the objects were written by specialists and often used terms familiar mainly to other specialists. The director did not want to lose accurate information. She wanted to discover why useful knowledge was failing to reach the visitors standing in front of it.

The education team observed visitors near a display of a wooden carrying box. The label began with the object's official name, its date, and a long description of the method used to join its parts. Most visitors looked at the box and moved on after reading the first few lines. Several thought it was a small table. The information was correct, but it did not explain early enough what the object had been used for. A person who understood the name could follow the rest. A person who did not understand it had to continue reading without knowing why the details mattered.

The team's first attempt at a new label was much shorter. It described the box as an object used to carry meals to people working away from home. Visitors understood its basic purpose more readily. However, a collection specialist pointed out a problem. The short text suggested that everyone in the region had used the same kind of box. The museum's records supported a narrower claim: this particular design appeared in a small group of communities. Removing a difficult phrase had also removed a useful limit. The team needed to explain the object clearly without turning a local example into a claim about a much wider population.

The second version used layers. A short opening sentence gave the carrying box's purpose in ordinary language. The next two sentences explained where this design had been recorded and why the handle made it easier to carry. A separate panel offered more detail about construction, including the specialist term and an explanation of it. Visitors could stop after learning the basic use or continue if they wanted technical information. The official object name remained on the label, but it no longer carried the whole burden of introducing the display. Short writing and full information became different stages of the same explanation.

To test the new labels, the museum invited groups of visitors to use part of the gallery with the old version and part with the new one. Staff asked what the objects were used for and which details visitors found useful. They did not simply ask whether the shorter text looked attractive. Nor did they count every minute spent standing beside an object as proof of understanding. A person might read slowly because the writing was confusing. The team compared what visitors could explain after reading. With the layered label, more people described the carrying box's purpose and recognized that its recorded use was limited to particular communities.

Not every result favored shorter introductions. At a display of woven cloth, some visitors wanted to know the meaning of a pattern before learning how the cloth was made. Others were interested mainly in the weaving process. A single sentence could not meet both needs. The team added a brief question at the start, inviting visitors to notice the repeated shape, followed by a clear explanation of what was known and what remained uncertain about its meaning. The technical account stayed available on the additional panel. The team treated the carrying box as a useful example, not as a template that every object had to follow exactly.

The museum also reviewed where its new panels were placed. A lower panel was easier for children and seated visitors to read, but a test position caused people to stand across a narrow route through the room. The team moved it beside a wider space and checked the text from different viewing positions. Digital information was considered, but the museum kept the main explanations on physical labels so visitors did not need a phone. Extra information could later be offered online. The director noted that accessible language was only one part of accessible explanation. A well-written text still failed if visitors could not comfortably find or read it.

After the trial, the museum revised labels across the household gallery in stages. Specialists checked accuracy, and education staff checked whether the opening made sense without prior knowledge. Visitor comments helped identify places needing further work. The director did not announce that every label should become as short as possible. Some subjects needed additional explanation, especially when a simple sentence risked removing an important limit. The goal was a useful path into accurate knowledge: start with what helps a visitor understand the object, then offer the evidence and detail behind that understanding. Changing the labels changed the order of the explanation rather than reducing the collection to a set of easy stories.

paragraphs.text: In the fictional town of Eastmere, a river separates a residential district from the market and railway station. The main road bridge carries cars, buses, bicycles, and pedestrians. During busy hours, traffic moves slowly, and people walking across it sometimes feel unsafe. The council proposed a new bicycle bridge beside an old riverside warehouse. Officials hoped that more cyclists would use the separate crossing, leaving more room on the main bridge. The proposal quickly attracted support and criticism. Some residents welcomed a safer route. Others argued that the town should spend the money on a wider road instead. At first, the debate relied mostly on personal accounts of inconvenient journeys.

A transport officer, Ben Shaw, asked the council to study who actually crossed the river and where they were going. Volunteers counted travelers at several times on weekdays and at weekends. They noted the direction of movement and whether people walked, cycled, or traveled in vehicles. They did not record names or attempt to identify individual drivers. The counts showed a large group of children and parents crossing toward the school each morning. They also showed cyclists heading for the station before the busiest shopping period. These journeys were not evenly spread through the day. A plan based only on afternoon car queues could miss important morning needs.

Ben then walked the proposed route with parents, cyclists, and a resident who used a wheelchair. The location beside the warehouse offered a short crossing of the water, but the paths on either side created problems. One path ended on a narrow street with delivery vehicles. The other climbed sharply before reaching the road to the station. Several cyclists said they might continue using the road bridge if the new route added a difficult climb and a long turn. Parents worried about meeting fast bicycles on a path that children would also use. Building a separate crossing did not automatically create a safe and convenient whole journey.

The council compared two possible locations. Moving the bridge upstream would increase the length of the structure and cost more. However, the paths there connected more directly with the school and station roads. A gradual approach could be built without the steep climb. The officer presented both the extra cost and the expected route benefits. He did not promise that every cyclist would change routes or that all car queues would disappear. The counts suggested that the crossing might serve existing walking and cycling journeys well. They could not show exactly how many drivers would later choose a bicycle instead of a car.

Another question concerned who would be allowed on the new bridge. Calling it a bicycle bridge had led several people to assume pedestrians would be excluded. The council instead considered a crossing for both walking and cycling, with clearly separated space where the width allowed. On the approaches, where space was tighter, signs would ask cyclists to slow down and give way. A parent argued that signs alone would not be enough near the school. The revised drawing therefore included a wider waiting area away from the cycle line at the school-side exit. This change responded to the observed morning pattern rather than to the busiest car period.

Supporters of a wider road still questioned the spending. They wanted to know whether the bridge would reduce congestion enough to justify its cost. Ben acknowledged that car travel mattered, but he asked the council to identify its main goal. If it wanted a safer and more direct crossing for children, pedestrians, and current cyclists, the survey supported the revised plan. If its main aim was to remove car queues, it needed additional evidence and perhaps a different project. Treating every possible benefit as guaranteed would make the bridge easier to advertise but harder to evaluate honestly after it opened.

The council chose to continue planning the upstream crossing, subject to a detailed cost review. It also decided to examine the main road bridge's crossings and signs rather than leave that bridge unchanged. Some residents would still need to use it, including people whose destinations did not fit the new route. The revised proposal described the new bridge as a shared river crossing, explained the waiting area, and showed how the paths connected to local roads. It no longer presented the project mainly as a way to cure traffic queues. Several original supporters disliked the more limited promise, while some parents who had opposed the warehouse location now supported the new route.

Eastmere had not yet built the bridge when the survey ended. The debate had nevertheless changed the plan. Counting crossings identified important journeys, and walking the routes revealed obstacles that a drawing of the river alone did not show. The council also learned that disagreement could involve different goals rather than different views of the same facts. A project useful for schoolchildren might not be the strongest project for reducing car delays. Deciding who should benefit required a public choice. The survey could inform that choice, but it could not make it for the town. A better proposal emerged when the council connected evidence about travel with a clear statement of what the bridge was meant to achieve.

choices.text: It clarified route obstacles, allowing the council to keep the cheaper location while widening its difficult approaches.

choices.text: It clarified morning travel needs, allowing the council to treat lower car delays as the bridge's main benefit.

questions.stem: Why was the upstream location considered despite its higher cost?

choices.text: It offered a shorter journey across the water with extra spending directed toward the delivery street's safety.
choices.text_ja: 川を渡る距離が短く、追加の費用を配送用の通りの安全対策に振り向けられたから。

choices.text: It offered a longer crossing with paths that could reach the station by retaining the existing steep approach.
choices.text_ja: 渡る距離は長いが、既存の急な取り付け道路を残したまま駅まで行ける道があったから。

choices.text: The upstream structure cost more but connected directly to useful roads and avoided the warehouse route's steep climb.
choices.text_ja: 上流の橋は費用が高いが、有用な道路に直接つながり、倉庫沿いのルートの急な上り坂を避けられたから。

choices.text: It offered clearer separation of walking and cycling space without needing changes to the connecting paths.
choices.text_ja: 取り付け道路を変えなくても、歩行者と自転車の空間をより明確に分けられたから。

questions.stem: What finding helped motivate the school-side waiting area?

choices.text_ja: 橋を共用する歩行者は、自転車が狭い川の横断部分を通り終えるまで待つ場所が必要だった。

choices.text: Morning crossings identified schoolchildren and parents needing space to wait clear of cyclists at the exit.
choices.text_ja: 朝の横断で、出口で自転車を避けて待つ場所を必要とする児童と保護者がいることが分かった。

choices.text: Cyclists heading for the station needed somewhere to wait before the main shopping traffic crossed the river.
choices.text_ja: 駅に向かう自転車利用者は、買い物客の主な通行が川を渡る前に待つ場所が必要だった。

choices.text: Parents walking the warehouse route needed a place to pause before entering the street used by deliveries.
choices.text_ja: 倉庫沿いのルートを歩く保護者は、配送車が使う通りに入る前に立ち止まる場所が必要だった。

questions.stem: Why did Ben ask the council to identify its main goal?

choices.text: The survey favored children and cyclists, so the council needed to decide how much car traffic to exclude.
choices.text_ja: 調査は子どもと自転車利用者に有利な結果だったので、議会はどれだけ自動車交通を締め出すかを決める必要があったから。

choices.text: The route comparisons favored the upstream site, but further counts were needed to identify its potential school users.

choices.text: The revised route could serve existing cyclists, but its higher cost made congestion relief necessary to justify it.

choices.text: To distinguish improvements to the design and its purpose from observed traffic or safety outcomes after construction.

choices.text: To explain why the cost review would determine whether the revised design actually met schoolchildren's safety needs.
choices.text_ja: 費用の見直しによって、修正した設計が児童の安全上の必要を実際に満たすかどうかが決まる理由を説明するため。
